description: I'm passionate about programming, robotics, AI, and cybersecurity. I enjoy solving problems, learning new technologies, and building innovative projects. I'm looking for creative, motivated, and collaborative team members with skills in programming, UI/UX design, AI, or project development who are excited to turn ideas into reality.
summary:
We built ChainSa to make NASA satellite data easier to explore and understand in the context of Myanmar. It is a web-based platform where users can look at environmental conditions through interactive maps, charts, and an AI assistant. The project brings together data from six areas: agriculture, disaster monitoring, the environment, water resources, energy, and urban development. Users can choose a township or location, view available observations, and compare changes over time.
We started this project because useful environmental data is often spread across different sources and can be difficult for people without technical experience to work with. ChainSa brings these datasets together in one place and explains the information in a more accessible way. We hope it can help students, researchers, local communities, and decision-makers better understand what is happening in their areas and use reliable information when making decisions about environmental challenges.
details:
ChainSa (Earth Trend Detective)

We created ChainSa to help people in Myanmar understand environmental changes using NASA satellite data. We noticed that this kind of information is often spread across different websites and can be difficult to understand without a technical background. So, we wanted to bring useful information together in one place and make it easier for people to explore. The platform supports both Burmese and English.

Users can choose from 38 environmental indicators across six areas: agriculture, disaster monitoring, environmental change, urban development, water resources, and energy. They can select a township or a reference location, choose an indicator, and set a date range. The results appear on an interactive map and charts, along with details such as the data source, observation dates, units, and limitations. We also explain whether the information represents a specific point, a group of satellite pixels, a river section, or an average for a township or region. When observations are missing, we leave them blank instead of treating them as zero.

Another important part of the project is our AI assistant. Users can ask questions in Burmese or English about environmental conditions and the data shown on the platform. The assistant helps explain the observations and their possible impacts. However, we do not want it to make claims that the data cannot support. For example, satellite observations are not the same as weather forecasts. For future weather information, we direct users to official forecasts from Myanmar's Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH).

We hope ChainSa will be useful to farmers, students, researchers, local communities, NGOs, and people involved in planning and decision-making. Instead of having to search through many different sources, they can explore several types of environmental information in one place and get a better picture of what is happening in their area.

We built the platform using HTML, CSS, TypeScript, Next.js, and React. We use Leaflet for interactive maps, Tailwind CSS for styling, Zod for data validation, Lucide for icons, and Vitest for automated testing. Our data sources include NASA POWER, MODIS products accessed through ORNL DAAC, NASA FIRMS, SWOT data through PO.DAAC Hydrocron, PACE OCI, and Black Marble through NASA LAADS DAAC. The AI assistant uses free models through OpenRouter, with Groq as a backup.

One feature that makes our project different is EARTH BEAT. It turns environmental data trends into sound, giving users another way to experience changes in the data. We also developed ways to derive surface-water and flood indicators from MODIS observations, identify urban areas for vegetation and temperature analysis, and estimate illuminated areas using Black Marble satellite pixels.

We spent time checking the data rather than simply displaying whatever the satellite products returned. For example, we found a discontinuity around 2008 in NASA POWER data over Myanmar. Because of this, we chose 2009–2025 as our comparison baseline and documented the reason. We also tested different nighttime-light thresholds against observations from Myanmar before choosing 2 nW·cm⁻²·sr⁻¹ as our main threshold. Lower thresholds could overestimate illuminated areas during the dry season.

We also considered the limitations of satellite data throughout development. Aerosol optical depth should not be presented as PM2.5, nighttime brightness does not directly show whether people have access to electricity, and satellite observations alone cannot predict future disasters. We want users to understand both what the data tells them and what it cannot tell them.

We developed and tested the project on standard laptop computers using free services, without relying on paid APIs or enabling billing. We also keep API credentials on the server instead of exposing them in the browser.

Our main goal is to make NASA Earth observation data easier to explore and understand, and to give people in Myanmar another useful way to learn about changes in their environment.
